extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers in combinatorics/convex/discrete geometry reading 'Proofs from THE BOOK'
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and following rigorous proofs in combinatorial and convex geometry (neighborly simplices, obtuse-angle problems, Borsuk's conjecture), using combinatorial counting, probabilistic methods, algebraic/number-theoretic lemmas, and geometric constructions. The material shows concrete constructions and general techniques to bound maximal sizes and produce counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct ±1-vector counting bound
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a matrix B we create a matrix C by replacing each zero entry by either +1 or −1, then each row of C is a (±1)-vector of length s and distinct rows imply C can have at most 2^s rows; using that not all (±1)-vectors appear yields a strict inequality and a bound r < 2^{d+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count distinct rows after replacing zeros by ±1. Distinctness arises either because replacements differ (same source row) or because original rows of B differ. Compare with total number 2^s of possible (±1)-vectors to obtain the inequality; note argument gives strict inequality because some (±1)-vectors cannot occur (they correspond to halfspace intersections not contained in any simplex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rows as intersections of halfspaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Each (±1)-row corresponds to an intersection of halfspaces (via formula (*)), so the set of representable (±1)-vectors corresponds exactly to those halfspace intersections that are subsets of some simplex Pi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a (±1)-vector does not occur in C, pick a point x not on any hyperplane Hj and not in any Pi; the (±1)-vector recording which sides of Hj contain x yields a halfspace intersection containing x and therefore cannot be contained in any Pi, so that vector is absent from C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing strips via hyperplanes orthogonal to edges
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point set S has no obtuse angles, then for any two points si, sj define Hij as the hyperplane through the origin orthogonal to si−sj, and the strip between Hij + si and Hij + sj contains all of S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define Hij = {x : ⟨x, si−sj⟩ = 0} and take its translates through si and sj. The strip contains exactly those x for which angles at si or sj with x are non-obtuse, so absence of obtuse angles implies the whole S lies inside the strip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence between strip containment and translates touching/intersecting
rubrics_metrics.description: P is contained in the strip between Hij + si and Hij + sj iff the translates P −si and P −sj lie in different halfspaces wrt Hij; from si ∈ P we get that all P −si contain the origin, so the P −si intersect in 0 but their interiors are pairwise disjoint (they only touch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate both the polytope and hyperplanes by −sj (or −si) to check halfspace containment equivalently. Use si ∈ conv(S) to conclude common intersection at 0. This constructs a correspondence between non-obtuse-angle sets and translates of P that intersect in a point but only touch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation to pairwise touching translates
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition 'translates intersect in a common point but only touch' is stronger than 'translates touch pairwise'; thus one may relax to the weaker condition of pairwise touching when deriving upper bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace P by any convex d-polytope Q and S by −S if convenient; pairwise touching is easier to satisfy and still suffices for the chain of inequalities leading to the bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski symmetrization preserves intersection and touching
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing a convex set Q by its Minkowski symmetrization Q* = {1/2(x−y): x,y∈Q} (centrally symmetric convex body) preserves whether two translates intersect, and preserves whether they touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show equivalence: (Q*+si)∩(Q*+sj) ≠ ∅ ⇔ (Q+si)∩(Q+sj) ≠ ∅ by expressing intersection points via sums/differences of points in Q. For touching, use the characterization that touching is intersection but remains non-intersecting after arbitrarily small translations along sj−si.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling and volume packing bound (factor 1/2 leads to 2^d)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Pj := 1/2(P + sj) are scaled translates of P contained in P and they only touch pairwise, then vol(Pj) = 1/2^d vol(P), so at most 2^d such sets fit into P, giving |S| ≤ 2^d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use convexity to show Pj ⊆ P; compute volume scaling by factor 1/2 for d-dimensional sets. The disjoint-interior condition implies the sum of volumes of Pj ≤ vol(P), giving the 2^d upper bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic existence via linearity of expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct large sets of 0/1-vectors with only acute angles, pick many random 0/1 vectors independently; define 'bad' triples (those producing right angles). Compute expected number of bad triples using the probability a fixed triple is bad, and use linearity of expectation to guarantee a choice with at most the expected number, allowing removal to obtain a good set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 3m random 0/1-vectors, a specific ordered triple (i,j,k) is bad with probability (3/4)^d. The expected number of bad triples equals (#triples)·(3/4)^d; choose m so this expectation < m, then remove ≤ m vectors to eliminate all bad triples, leaving 2m vectors with only acute angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability computation for right-angle occurrence among 0/1-vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Three 0/1-vectors x(i),x(j),x(k) determine a right angle at x(j) iff for every coordinate ℓ either x(i)ℓ−x(j)ℓ = 0 or x(k)ℓ−x(j)ℓ = 0; the probability a specific triple is bad is (3/4)^d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each coordinate there are 8 equally likely patterns for (x(i)ℓ, x(j)ℓ, x(k)ℓ); 6 of these are 'bad' in the sense described, so per coordinate probability 3/4. Independence across coordinates (product) yields (3/4)^d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Markov's inequality and expectation tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic probabilistic tools used: finite probability space definition, random variables, linearity of expectation (no independence required), and Markov's inequality Prob(X ≥ a) ≤ EX / a for nonnegative X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linearity of expectation is used to bound expected number of bad triples; Markov's inequality is listed as the third tool (useful when bounding tail probabilities from expectations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter selection for probabilistic construction (choice of m)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose m = floor( √( (6/9) 2 / √3 ) d ) (as in the theorem) so that the combinatorial inequalities yield the expected number of bad triples < m, enabling removal of m vectors to leave 2m good vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit formula for m is used to ensure the combinatorial/inequality chain 3·C(3m,3)·(3/4)^d < m via the estimates shown. The exact constant can be adjusted with the same method; numerical evaluation yields explicit large examples (e.g., 72 points in d=34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct Q of ±1-vectors with parity constraint and nearly-orthogonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Q = {x ∈ {±1}^n : x1 = 1 and the number of −1 components is even}, so |Q| = 2^{n−2}, and for all x,y∈Q one has ⟨x,y⟩ ≡ 2 (mod 4); declare x,y nearly-orthogonal if |⟨x,y⟩| = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial constraint produces a structured set with constrained inner products; nearly-orthogonality corresponds to minimal nonzero inner products and is central to bounding distances in later matrix/vector constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial divisibility lemma using binomial representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define P(z) = C(z−2, q−2). P(z) is integer-valued for integer z and is divisible by p (where q = p^m) iff z ≢ 0 or 1 (mod q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the product form of binomial coefficients and compare p-adic valuations of numerator and denominator; analyze residue classes mod q to locate extra p-factors. This lemma is used to force divisibility properties when evaluating polynomials at certain inner-product-derived integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separating vectors via evaluation polynomials Fy(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: For y∈Q define Fy(x) := P( (⟨x,y⟩+2)/4 ). Then Fy(y)=1 while for x≠y in any Q′ without nearly-orthogonal pairs, Fy(x) is divisible by p. These polynomials thus separate y from other x by divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Fy as integer-valued polynomial; use the Lemma about P to deduce divisibility patterns. This produces a family of polynomials that behave like indicator functions modulo p for the chosen set Q′.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to n−1 variables and squarefree monomials linear independence bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute x1=1 and reduce higher powers x_i^2=1 (i>1) to get polynomials in n−1 variables of degree ≤ q−2 that are squarefree; linear independence of these polynomials implies |Q′| ≤ number of squarefree monomials = sum_{i=0}^{q−2} C(n−1,i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show no nontrivial rational linear relation among the Fy polynomials using divisibility at evaluations; conclude that the count of independent polynomials is at most the dimension of the vector space spanned by squarefree monomials of degree ≤ q−2, giving the combinatorial bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding into rank-1 matrices and inner product amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Map x∈Q to M(x)=xx^T (an n×n rank-1 matrix). Viewing matrices as vectors in R^{n^2}, one gets ⟨M(x),M(y)⟩ = ⟨x,y⟩^2 ≥ 4, with equality exactly when x,y are nearly-orthogonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This embedding amplifies small inner products to large positive values and allows geometric arguments (distances/angles) in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space; minimal scalar product corresponds to nearly-orthogonal original vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extracting subdiagonal-vector representation S and diameter characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: From M(x) take U(x) ∈ {±1}^d as the vector of subdiagonal entries; the set S of these U(x) has size 2^{n−2}. The maximal distance between points in S is attained exactly for nearly-orthogonal pairs, so any subset of smaller diameter than S is bounded in size by the previously derived combinatorial bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate ⟨M(x),M(y)⟩ to ⟨U(x),U(y)⟩ via the identity ⟨M(x),M(y)⟩ = 2⟨U(x),U(y)⟩ + n. Use equal length of U(x) to deduce when distances are maximal; transfer the earlier combinatorial limit to a bound on parts in a diameter-reducing partition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic estimates via monotonicity, unimodality, and Stirling-type bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use monotonicity and unimodality of binomial coefficients and factorial bounds n! > e (n/e)^n and n! < e n (n/e)^n to estimate combinatorial sums and derive asymptotic lower bounds like f(d) > (1.2)√d for large d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace sums of binomials by a single dominating term with combinatorial approximations, apply factorial bounds, and manipulate inequalities to get exponential-type lower bounds; use these to conclude existence of counterexamples in specified dimensions (e.g., q=9 → d=561).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall methodological principle: reduce geometric/packing problems to algebraic/combinatorial constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The proofs proceed by translating geometric partition/packing/touching questions into combinatorial counts, linear algebraic embeddings, polynomial divisibility constraints, or probabilistic expectations, and then applying counting/number-theoretic/expectation bounds to obtain existence or nonexistence results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: construct/identify a combinatorial object encoding geometry (±1-vectors, matrices, subdiagonals), establish algebraic properties (inner products mod constraints, divisibility), use linear independence or expectation to bound sizes, and translate back to geometric conclusions (maximal number of points, counterexamples).
